To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the fold of protein G is completely defined when its dihedral angles are known to within 1 °, that a few long‐distance contacts constrain the fold much better than a complete, accurate set of dihedral restructures, and that TAD/SA simulations using hydrogen‐bond, idealized dihedrals, and hydrophobic distance restrains are a practical approach to protein structure calculation.

(i) TAD/SA simulations of protein G using dihedral re­ straints are not very successful, but that (ii) simulations using hydrogen‐bond and hydrophobic re­ strains are successful, and that (iii) the hydrophobic restrains can be used to obtain the correct fold when the hydrogen bonds and dihedral angles are not available.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods to determine the structures of biological molecules from limited data.
the development of a strategy for structure calculation of proteins from limited data.
the use of limited experimental data in protein structure calculations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a complete set of dihedral angles for all residues in a protein is not sufficient for the calculation of its three‐dimensional structure.
the X‐ray crystal structure of a protein is not completely defined by the dihedral angle values.
the structure of a protein is determined when the positions of its backbone atoms are known.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that a combination of hydrogen‐bond, secondary structure, and hydrophobic re‐strains, derived from limited experimental data, can provide a good starting structure for refinement.

the structure of a protein can be calculated from a few long‐ and short‐range restraints, and the calculation can be done using the same force fields and protocols used for calculations with complete data sets.
the structure of a protein can be determined with high accuracy by combining experimental data with a model of the structure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a few long‐ range contacts can constrain the fold better that a complete set of all‐ atom restraints, and that the fold is more sensitive to violations of hydrogen bonds than to dihedral angles.
a small set of long‐range restraints can constrain a protein to a fold that is close to the native fold.

it is possible to obtain a good approximation to the native fold of a protein by combining a limited set of restraints derived from sequence, secondary structure, and long‐range contacts, with a small set of accurate restraints derived from NMR data.
